text: Our new stigma research looks at diabetes stigma at scale across the UK. With blame, shame and stigma staggeringly high across type 1 diabetes and type 2 diabetes – what can be done to tackle it? There’s an article following publication of a new survey here: 86% of people with type 1 and 75% of people with type 2 experience judgement for their condition Nobody should experience judgment or blame because of a health condition. But our new survey, conducted by YouGov and kindly funded by Abbott shows almost 9 in 10 people with type 1 diabetes and 7 in 10 people with type 2 diabetes experience blame and judgement for their condition. www.diabetes.org.uk And the 2025 Diabetes UK Position Statement on Stigma is here

Well done @everydayups and downs, for bringing this to everyone's attention. For what it is worth  here is my experience and opinion. There is a T2DM crisis and the NHS is struggling to cope with it. It seems to me that the Department of Health and the NHS bureaucracy are using "nudge techniques" to get every one to change their behaviour. What better way of doing this than blaming being overweight or obese for your contracting T2DM. The deadly diabetes grim reaper will come for you if you don't lose weight. I believe that the stigma which diabetics feel is applied to them is connected to the distress that many new members to this forum write about. Anyone who is overweight is a likely candidate for diabetes so avoid eating sweets, biscuits, potato chips and croissants and everything will be OK. Well it won't be ok, contracting diabetes is a complex issue concerning age, genetics, exercise and other criteria not just being overweight. So how do you "nudge" people into rejuvenating themselves or changing their genetic make up, to reduce the incidence of T2DM? You can't, so blame being overweight. It is time that the Department of Health and the media wake up to the fact that stigmatising people does not help. The public need genuine facts to make their health judgements not public relations blandishments. It is true that a fair proportion of diabetics were overweight, whatever that means, when they were diagnosed, but a small proportion of diabetics were underweight. Does it mean, however, that people who are underweight are condemned to contract diabetes? Is there stigma against light people too? It is clear that "nudging" people to lose weight is not working as T2DM has almost become an epidemic. Perhaps a new approach is needed. The "nudge" campaign to get people to stop smoking worked and it helped to reduce lung cancer and other respiratory problems, but it was clear to most people that smoking was directly related to lung cancer and the evidence was overwhelming. There is no clear cut single cause of diabetes, so why blame being overweight alone? The NHS is full of hardworking and qualified staff,  and my life was saved by some of them when I contracted a lung abscess which was fully resolved by antibiotics. The treatment for diabetes is entirely different, as there is no magic wand that can be waved either to prevent diabetes or to cure it. It is down to wise decision making about diet, exercise and medication. Unfortunately, the NHS doctors are run off their feet and many of them have been poorly trained to meet the needs of their patients. It is not just a case of everyone losing weight and everything will be ok. Take my own case, when I contracted T2DM I was not overweight and I exercised every day. I did more than my fair share of walking and running. I still got diabetes, probably and primarily because of my age,73, and genetics. Diabetes runs in my family so many of us have the genes that predispose us to diabetes, when we get to a certain age, and some of us do not have the genes that protect us. Should we be blamed for being old or having "weak" genes? Many, many people who are overweight do not contract diabetes  because they have a physique which does not lend itself to poor regulation of blood sugar. To get to remission I have had to take drastic measures to control my diet and exercise routines, and I have had to lose weight and reduce my waist measurement. Perhaps, continuously, and all of my life, being 62kg with a waist measurement of 80 cm and with a BMI of 19.6  would have prevented me from becoming a diabetic, but the result would have been the same: I would have been on a continuous low carb diet and exercising by walking 10 km per day, just as I  am now. It is a bitter irony. Lots of the health professional I have met have considered me to be too thin and they think I should put a bit of weight on; just in case I contract an abscess again or cancer and I need an operation. I am afraid that they cannot have their" low-weight patient" cake and eat it. I debated with the doctors whether it was the abscess that brought on my  full diabetes or whether the the diabetes caused the abscess. Some of them believed the diabetes damaged my immune system; it was blame diabetes again. Luckily, my GP is not part of the blame culture. Of course, being overweight is problematic for younger people and it contributes to their demise. However, where is the stigma against the ultra high processed foods and the advertising which encourages over indulgence? Where is the stigma against the Forever Chemicals which are polluting the whole of our environment and which are increasingly being seen as being another causative factor of T2DM? Society must stop the blame culture and stop insulting people who are overweight by calling them obese, and stop blaming diabetics for being overweight. None of this stigma is helping anybody and it leads to stress which exacerbates the condition even more. It is very difficult living with the physical effects of diabetes and regulating the condition, but sometimes it is more difficult dealing with the mental effects. No more stigma please, hard working NHS staff are run off their feet and do not have time to treat you as an individual rather than a stigmatised member of an overweight herd.

On The Pills, my weight went higher and higher and no dieting was making any difference, I was hardly eating anything, no weight loss - PILLS have a lot to answer for. I’d had a bad illness just before covid was officially announced, it was 6 weeks after ‘a covid’ booster jab. Then, in 2023 diagnosed whi Haemochromatosis Compound variant, Type 1, Celtic disease. Inherited Liver disorder, read up on that! Shocked to my core that ‘I’ a Complementary Health care Therapist of many years, had very basic knowledge of ‘Dire betes’ got it!! I am sick to my back teeth of people saying ‘You can reverse it with THAT diet’!! I had gone very low carb higher protein and I have NOT reversed it or as should be said put it into ‘Remission’!! I’m still fighting like many to keep my BG as low as I can…. So - I have PAF, GH, T2 ‘dire betes’ and that hasn’t been all sadly Mental health - what’s that? Not in a good place at the moment and suffering anxiety….. Panicky like feelings. No one wants to know, family get AND to add to all this, It’s nigh on impossible to eat anywhere other than home! No one considers a Low Carb diabetics dietary needs in cafes, restaurants, residential courses you name it. WHY is this???? Yes, I spoke to the catering, 2/3 days I was not being listened to - TILL one night BG gone so low I was frighted to go to bed……. There is still no definitive answer as to why anyone contracts Type1 or Type2 diabetes. Type 1 is often referred to as an auto-immune disease where the pancreas "stops itself" from producing insulin. The cause of this auto-immune disease could be because of genetic factors or even virus infection or both together. There can be no possible reason why anyone could be blamed  if they contract Type1. The causes of Type 2 diabetes are different and more complicated and multi-factorial, but once again genetics plays an important role, as do environmental factors and your age: also diet, weight and exercise are factors but not the only ones. Regulating your diet, weight and exercise is probably more important after you contract the condition than before. There can be no excuse for blaming a Type 2 diabetic by saying they eat too much, are too heavy or don't exercise enough. Most people "eat too much, weigh too much and do not exercise enough" in the opinion of NHS, but most people do not contract Type 2 so there must be other factors involved. The age at which many people contract Type 2 is now falling, so we need research to find out why. Environmental factors could be crucial; we are all being exposed to "forever chemicals" and micro-plastics and ultra-high-processed foods. Younger people are being exposed to more stress. There is even research that suggests that too much light at the wrong time of day has an adverse effect on our endocrine system. Genetics could predispose you, and then environmental factors could push you over the edge. We owe it to younger people to improve their environment to ensure that they have happy, productive and long lives. Stigma does not help any diabetic. The only way to ameliorate the problem would be to establish the full facts and use reason to find solutions.

I’ve received thanks for the forum, and you @Northerner for bringing this card to the attention of Diabetes UK. They certainly jumped into action, and the card was withdrawn from sale very quickly. I’ve had this official response to share with you, that gives more information: “Thank you for bringing to our attention this issue. Diabetes is not a joke, and this card fuels the blame, judgement and harmful misconceptions that people with diabetes face on a daily basis. First and foremost we hope that you are ok, and would like to remind you that if you do need our support you can reach out to our helpline at 0345 123 2399. ​ ​ “We want to reassure you that Tesco have confirmed that the card has been removed from sale and have apologised for the offence caused. The card was sold by a third-party seller on Tesco Marketplace, and Tesco have reassured us that they have strict guidelines in place that they expect all third-party sellers to follow, alongside internal processes in place to monitor for any products that do not align with these standards. They are sorry that on this occasion this did not happen, and are working to immediately address this issue through an internal investigation. Diabetes UK and Tesco have a longstanding partnership and have been working together for over a decade to fight against diabetes stigma and remain committed to doing so. We are pleased that following action by Tesco, the card has also been removed from other retail outlets. ​ ​ “At Diabetes UK we remain committed to tackling diabetes stigma, and will continue to challenge the myths and misinformation that fuel it. We also know we can’t do this alone, so would like to thank you for bringing this to our attention so that we can strike out stigma.” ​

Saw this on Facebook, from the father of Lyla (who died from undiagnosed Type 1) - there was a scene in Coronation Street last night exactly as was described - I don't watch it but made a point of looking at it on ITV X - not very good from ITV IMO Here is my email to Kate Brooks at ITV (in charge of Corrie) Aaand relax #LylaLaw #T1D #Diabetes #fyp Dear Kate, I am writing regarding Summer’s storyline in last night’s episode of Coronation Street. While I understand the intention behind portraying her becoming drunk from sugary alcoholic drinks, the way the scene concluded, with the line “I’m hyper… erm, hypo, I need insulin.” was deeply concerning. Administering insulin during a hypoglycaemic episode is extremely dangerous and can be fatal. If someone is experiencing a hypo, they require glucose, not insulin. A more accurate and safer way to portray this would have been for Summer to say she needed to check her levels before determining what action to take. Ending the scene with “I’m hypo, I need insulin” risks confusing the public and reinforcing harmful misconceptions. Even reversing the order of the words “I’m hypo… erm, hyper, I need insulin” would have been less damaging. I fully appreciate that Coronation Street is a drama, but it is also one of the most influential programmes in the UK. With that influence comes a responsibility to portray medical conditions accurately. Misrepresentation further contributes to stigma, misunderstanding, and in the case of Type 1 Diabetes, potentially dangerous assumptions. This issue is profoundly personal to me, as well as to the hundreds of thousands of people living with Type 1 Diabetes across the UK. My daughter, Lyla Story, died at just two years old from undiagnosed Type 1 Diabetes in May last year. Her death was preventable. Since then, I have dedicated myself to campaigning nationally for Lyla’s Law, which seeks to address the systemic failures that continue to put children and adults at risk. The campaign focuses on: 1. Accountability for missed diagnoses in primary care 2. Mandatory education for all healthcare professionals, especially GPs 3. National public awareness of the 4Ts — Toilet, Thirsty, Tired, Thinner Given the seriousness of this condition, the rising number of diagnoses, and the urgent need for accurate public education, I respectfully ask that Summer’s character and her experience of living with Type 1 Diabetes are portrayed in a more accurate and realistic manner going forward. Lives genuinely depend on public understanding. Thank you for taking the time to consider this important matter. I would welcome the opportunity to discuss this further and to share more about Lyla’s Law and the work being done to prevent future tragedies. With warm regards, Mr. John Paul Story Did anyone see it?

I agree wholeheartedly. Public knowledge and appreciation of the condition needs to improve across the board including the internet's social media. We must all be dealing with the facts. However, what is really disturbing is the appalling lack of knowledge and trained staff to deal with all forms of diabetes. It is estimated that there are 6 million people, in the UK, with some form of diabetes and at least 10% of them have type 1.  This means that there are 600,000 people with a condition which can only be treated with insulin, and there is no remission or mitigation for them.  They need all the support they can get. When my Mother contracted Type 1 in the 1960s, there were clinics readily available which were staffed with experienced professionals, she did not need to do her own research as advice and education were available all the time. We are richer now but the resources are not available to give adequate support. Surely, it is not beyond the wit of our society to reduce the number of people who are suffering from type 2. If we could get those numbers down then we could concentrate on  type1 diabetics who can do very little or nothing to prevent themselves contracting a serious disease.

Moderator Note: These posts were split from an earlier thread to give this topic its own space. It’s nigh on impossible to eat anywhere other than home! No one considers a Low Carb diabetics dietary needs in cafes, restaurants, residential courses you name it. WHY is this???? Last July I attended a residential course where the venue organisers said you are not to bring your own food, they will cater! Yeah right…… So I trusted them, did they cater for my needs??? NO, numbers going through the floor because I wasn’t getting enough to eat and nothing I could buy in house. Yes, I spoke to the catering, 2/3 days I was not being listened to - TILL one night BG gone so low I was frighted to go to bed……. I had a lady who took me to get some foods, so walked long way to fridge to get some. Didn’t work quickly enough and a member of staff was worried, had phoned the manager at 11;30pm! Only then taken seriously!

Hello there, My Type 2 turned up virtually overnight  too, but I have lots of family members with type 2 and my mother had Type 1. It has been very difficult for me to go into so called remission, and I am not certain now that I will pass the remission test when I have my HbA1c test in early November: I have had to lose a lot of weight and reduce my waist measurement, go on a low carb diet and do lots of exercise. Sometimes, I ask myself has it been worth it and should I have just stayed on the Sitagliptin and Metformin combination. I have had no help whatsoever from the diabetic clinic since my Blood Glucose Hba1c fell below 48mmo/mol. There is very little help anywhere; you have to do it yourself and do all the research yourself. This is where the forum and local group come in most handy. The Diabetes UK website and balance magazine are also a mine of useful information. I agree with what you say about restaurants, cafes, etc. and even hospital canteens. They are a desert as far as catering for diabetics is concerned. Diabetes professionals tell you that that you can eat any food you like - yes you can. However, if you try this approach then you have to seriously limit the quantity of what you eat or drink. If you eat too many plums, cherries or apples you will get a blood glucose spike. The same goes for other low glycaemic foods.  Its ok to get a temporary Blood Glucose spike but not every day. When I was in my twenties and thirties , I could eat what I liked and as much as I liked and when I liked- that is the privilege that non-diabetics are given by the natural hormonal regulation of the level of their blood glucose. Those of us who are diabetic or pre-diabetic or even in remission (from Type2) do not have this privilege. We consciously and constantly have to use measures to regulate the results of hormonal deficiencies. Eating a meal of food that is full of starch or sugar does not help any diabetic. It is difficult to find an eating house that considers the needs of diabetics , probably because it is too much trouble, and they couldn't care less. I find myself returning to places that meet my needs time and time again, and when someone suggests a new restaurant I carefully look at the menu before I go, all the spontaneity of eating out has been spoilt for me. Eating oysters is ok ; you can go for it if you have enough money. You can eat as much cheese and as many eggs as you like, but watch out for constipation and the cholesterol police. Diabetics need to take care, for they cannot do or eat as they like, without concern. It's a pity the rest of society does not recognise this. Good luck.

Diabetes is considered a disability…….. I get interesting replies from diabetics about this! ‘NICE guide lines’ So, if restaurants can cater for all the other dietary requirements/needs/wants then they certainly should cater for those diabetics who have to have Low Carb diet. Note that apparently they have a directive with 14 ‘allergens’ on but nothing about Low Carb, it’s not hard or rocket science. Many places round me are mostly fast food and have forgotten salad options. Son said ‘just ask for what you want’ ie: bit of this n that providing it in their menu…….. even that doesn’t work often. So……. Going on courses, holidays are a nightmare……..

The challenge with this is always that there isn’t one “diabetes diet”, and that not everyone finds low carb necessary, or indeed particularly helpful. On the forum we have lots of people with lots of different types of diabetes, and approaches to food vary widely. We have some people with T1 who find low carb helpful. And we have some people with T2 for whom low calorie is far more important than low carb (their pancreatic function has been largely restored by weight loss). Still others have diabetes and take medication that works best when balanced with the right amount of carbohydrate. And some people who choose to eat low carb, do so for other reasons than diabetes! I once ordered the ‘diabetic meal’ on a flight. Never again! Chosen and carefully put together by someone for a diabetes that was nothing like mine ! I suppose it’s a bit like vegetarian options. Not so long ago there would be a menu full of meat, and just one option if you were vegetarian. Take it or leave it! These days it’s much more common to have several enticing vegetarian options available. And often vegan choices too! Plus these days you often get lower calorie options identified on menus. I’d hope we will gradually move to menus which have more low carb options (including sides) to make it easier for folks on low carb diets to have a selection to choose from. Often on TV cooking shows (eg Masterchef) things are accompanied by Celeriac Mash, or other lower carb options. But personally I’d much prefer it if they made absolutely no mention of diabetes in relation to the low carb choices.

‘But personally I’d much prefer it if they made absolutely no mention of diabetes in relation to the low carb choices’ Ok, I understand you don’t want that, so how would you endeavour to get what you need? I believe there is a need in the catering industry to understand people who have these dietary needs as round my county they mostly don’t. This means as I’m sure you know, that I and others find it impossible to to eat out. It may be described as ‘Carb intolerance’ instead of Low Carb It wouldn’t be SO bad if they had proper plain food options, most have gone to cheap high carb fast foods. NICE say that Diabetes is classed as a disablement and therefore should have considerations. Restaurants, food outlets will cater for vegetarian, vegan etc but do not even consider diabetes. I do not believe they even know about it. Obviously the new issues for them now is those taking medications to lose weight and may not eat some foods on the menus. Also those needing low calorie would be catered for with good standard food choices. My point is, where ever I go to eat they do not know or understand ‘Low Carb’ diet is not just a dietary choice and I fail to understand why establishments do not know if they have been trained in the industry. The whole industry should be informed about Diabetes, there are those who need to inject, where do they go to do this? I’ve read people sit in toilet cubicles! I feel their embarrassment. I have been a qualified Complementary Health Care Therapist of 25yrs, I HAD to take Anatomy & Physiology to practice and CPD. I had to be mindful of those with Diabetes and act according to their needs. All down to public education..

As @everydayupsanddowns says, there is no one diabetic diet. I’m Type 1 and my diet is what I’d eat if I didn’t have diabetes. Moreover, it’s easy to identify and reduce/omit carbs if you choose too. A menu listing Baked Potato, chicken and salad clearly has carbs. You can either choose something else. Choose that meal but eat none/some of the potato, as you choose, or request the potato is substituted with another menu item, eg you might request two servings of salad or a serving of green veg instead. I have been T2 since 2013 and have never taken medication for it.   For the last 5+ (probably longer) I have been gluten-free, so that my way of eating is gluten-free low carb.  We are a foodie household and my OH is an excellent cook is neither low carb, nor does he have to be glute-free. My approach to eating out is to look for something suitable that I fancy, but if there's nothing, I choose the least worst option from the menu.  I'm rarely going to be a prisoner to any alien kitchen's offerings for more than a day or two. When diagnosed, my OH and I made a pact.  That agreement was that for our main meals of the day, if we are eating at home, we share the same meal, and secondly that I do not avoid or decline invitations to functions/events on that basis of dietary requirements. At home, this means he will have carbier sides, or more of any of the carbier things I might be having a small portion of. If we're going to something where I have zero idea on what will be served, I will usually have a piece of cheese or something before we leave - to potentially keep the wolf from the door.  If there's nothing I fancy, I just don't eat. If it's finger food, I can sometimes be mingling with something like a small sarnie or a sausage roll on a plate, but never touching it.  I prefer the sausage roll option as I can tear it in two and it looks like I've been eating.  Fillings of sandwiches have been eater, without eating the bread, although I have to be a bit careful with that. Of course, I have a few miles on my diabetes clock, but I can assure you that back in 2013 the notion of low carb eating was somewhat unusual, and on some diabetes forums one would be lectured  on how unhealthy low carb eating is.  The Eatwell Plate was very much the order of the day. As I say, I'm long-term into meds free T2, but I see no shame in meds.  For me, if I needed to consider medication I would.  There are far worse things than medication, if it helps me live my life in a way I find acceptable. I do have concerns about hospitalisation, although my OH have both agreed if the other has to have inpatient treatment, the other will bring decent food.

Levemir is a basal (background) insulin, so similar to the Tresiba you use but Levemir is shorter acting and more flexible and is usually injected twice a day, morning and evening. Sadly for those using it, it is being discontinued by the manufacturer. Tresiba would not suit some of us because it is so long acting, as we need to adjust our basal doses for exercise and hormonal changes etc. For example I need a lot more Levemir in the morning (22u) than at night (about 3u) and if I have done exercise during the day then I need to reduce my small evening dose accordingly or I have nocturnal hypos. I would not be able to do this with Tresiba because it lasts about 36hours and each dose tops up the previous one and any adjustment you do affects the day and night and takes about 3 days to have it's full effect whereas I need to change my evening dose much more regularly and sometimes consecutive nights for several nights, either down or up if I haven't exercised.

Celtic38 said: Hello is Diabetes Type 3c a rare condition then because I have not come across that it much, hope you don't mind me asking you this question. Click to expand... No problem, @Celtic 38. Yes a T3c diagnosis is still pretty infrequent and comes from damage to the pancreas leading to elevated BG - other than the formally recognised auto-immune conditions for T1. Consequently treatment paths can vary from "as if T2" and treat with oral meds; "as if T2" and treat with some insulin as well as oral meds; or "as if T1" and treat with full MDI or a pump. The panc'y damage can be from a physical accident, alcohol excess, steroid excess, pancreatitis, partial panc'y surgery, and in my case a full pancreatectomy to deal with pancreatic cancer. Until recent years T3c was barely recognised by the NHS or Health Care Professionals (HCPs) and I suspect a no of people with panc'y damage were misdiagnosed as T2 or T1. After my surgery I was discharged as T1 (but clearly didn't have the autoimmune condition). The poor recognition of T3c continues, but is improving. The relevance is that most T3c patients are managing a seperate ailment from their panc'y damage, which often needs precedence over their diabetes treatment plan. In my case I can't estimate my insulin doses sufficiently well IF I'm not digesting fully what I eat; gastro probs post surgery 5+ yrs ago continue to interfere with my digestion. I also need a Pancreatic Enzyme Replacement Therapy (PERT) because I no longer create any significant digestive enzymes. My medication for that is Creon capsules; there are other similar capsules. PERT is not unique to those with D from panc'y damage; it's also a remedy for other gastro problems. But many T3cs need PERT. With an ailment such as pancreatitis flare ups can be quite isolated, treated and managed for a while afterwards then a repeat flare up. Gradual worsening may continue until a more abrupt failure of their panc'y - but without the medical recognition that their recent D diagnosis has a fundamentally different cause of pancreatitis: neither high insulin resistance nor an autoimmune status. Overall T1s are c. 10% of the D community, T2s are c. 90% and less than 1% are all of the rest, including gestational D. Those %s are possibly now slightly out of date, with the recent increased acceptance that T3c is real. Over 30 x T3cs have registered on this forum which is probably unrepresentative of the UK wide D community and many arrived here because they had or still have problems with getting the right diagnosis or a poorly provided treatment path. The Forum has provided somewhere to reach out to for help. In the final analysis a diagnosis of D Type comes from the cause of that D.

Celtic38 said: Hello is Diabetes Type 3c a rare condition then because I have not come across that it much, hope you don't mind me asking you this question. Click to expand... No problem, @Celtic 38. Yes a T3c diagnosis is still pretty infrequent and comes from damage to the pancreas leading to elevated BG - other than the formally recognised auto-immune conditions for T1. Consequently treatment paths can vary from "as if T2" and treat with oral meds; "as if T2" and treat with some insulin as well as oral meds; or "as if T1" and treat with full MDI or a pump. The panc'y damage can be from a physical accident, alcohol excess, steroid excess, pancreatitis, partial panc'y surgery, and in my case a full pancreatectomy to deal with pancreatic cancer. Until recent years T3c was barely recognised by the NHS or Health Care Professionals (HCPs) and I suspect a no of people with panc'y damage were misdiagnosed as T2 or T1. After my surgery I was discharged as T1 (but clearly didn't have the autoimmune condition). The poor recognition of T3c continues, but is improving. The relevance is that most T3c patients are managing a seperate ailment from their panc'y damage, which often needs precedence over their diabetes treatment plan. In my case I can't estimate my insulin doses sufficiently well IF I'm not digesting fully what I eat; gastro probs post surgery 5+ yrs ago continue to interfere with my digestion. I also need a Pancreatic Enzyme Replacement Therapy (PERT) because I no longer create any significant digestive enzymes. My medication for that is Creon capsules; there are other similar capsules. PERT is not unique to those with D from panc'y damage; it's also a remedy for other gastro problems. But many T3cs need PERT. With an ailment such as pancreatitis flare ups can be quite isolated, treated and managed for a while afterwards then a repeat flare up. Gradual worsening may continue until a more abrupt failure of their panc'y - but without the medical recognition that their recent D diagnosis has a fundamentally different cause of pancreatitis: neither high insulin resistance nor an autoimmune status. Overall T1s are c. 10% of the D community, T2s are c. 90% and less than 1% are all of the rest, including gestational D. Those %s are possibly now slightly out of date, with the recent increased acceptance that T3c is real. Over 30 x T3cs have registered on this forum which is probably unrepresentative of the UK wide D community and many arrived here because they had or still have problems with getting the right diagnosis or a poorly provided treatment path. The Forum has provided somewhere to reach out to for help. In the final analysis a diagnosis of D Type comes from the cause of that D.

The mods, hosts and DUK staff have been discussing AI recently. And how it fits into the ethos of the forum. The forum is a space for peer support, the sharing of lived human experiences, and encouragement. However we recognise that AI can be helpful for some members for a number of reasons - perhaps particularly those with neurodiversity or langauge difficulties, or to summarise a long document. Consequently an outright ban on use of AI does not seem appropriate. However AI-generated posts can feel cold and impersonal, lack the authenticity of lived experience, and are prone to factual errors. As a result a new user guideline has been added (please do check the user guidelines), requiring that members clearly identify posts which have been written with the assistance (or entirely) by AI. Our recommendation is to use AI as sparingly as possible to keep the human-interaction of the forum paramount. ALL AI generated posts must now be clearly identified. For example: “I asked [AI engine] for a summary of [prompt], and this was the result: [AI generated text] ” Or “[Paste of AI Text in italics]” AI Generated Important Note: Posts which are or appear to be AI Generated which are not clearly marked as such may be deleted or quarantined. Consistent violations of forum rules may lead to your user account being limited or banned - see forum rules for details. Thanks for your cooperation in keeping the forum a friendly, supportive, and above all human-centred place.

The same literature will be reviewed, and those doing it will be aware of guidance elsewhere, and quite possibly know the people on those panels (having met at international conferences, read studies they have published etc). Guideline Development Groups at NICE (I was a lay member for T1 guideline update) comprise healthcare professionals, researchers, statisticians, pharmacists, plus editors / representatives of the guideline body itself who know the NICE process inside out. The panel will also be aware of guidelines across the world, and where changes are being considered, the evidence for them and the potential ‘ripple effect’ will be very carefully considered. Eg when the HbA1c target was altered / reworded in 2015 - the headline number dropping from aim for 7.5% to aim for 6.5%. It was recognised that other countries may consider following suit. What is crucial though is that national guidance is far less usable in other healthcare contexts, even when they are only recommendations. Your Dr is less likely to be interested what the latest advice is in Australia. And where guidance becomes financially binding (such as a Technology Appraisal) the local budget holders won’t care what sensors must be made available to whom in Germany or France etc etc. If I am refused something I can discuss NICE guidance and recommendations with my Dr or Clinic, and ask why they aren’t following it… But they would be much freer to shrug off recommendations by the ADA in the US or whatever.

I've had the same with my OH's CRV.  I tried the tank additive and a long drive at high RPM which didn't work so I bought some of this stuff on the recommendation of our mechanic: https://www.amazon.co.uk/JLM-Diesel-DPF-Spray/dp/B0191OMGW0?s=automotive&sr=1-33 It needs to go into the DPF directly when the system is cool (easy on the CRV, just disconnect the two rubber tubes from the pressure differential sensor and find out which one has some back pressure in it, then squirt it down that) into the end of the DPF nearest the engine.  Squirt the whole can in, leave it to soak in for 20 minutes, then start the engine and let the car warm up.  Once it's starting to warm raise the rpm to 3000 or so and hold it there.  After a while you'll see a load of smoke appear (not quite battleship obscuring but still a lot) keep going until that stops - it won't hurt to keep the revs up for longer than that and may even help.  You may see a load of black frothy gunk appear from the tailpipe, it's harmless and will clear away with a bucket of water.  This stuff really works!   Depending on your car's engine management system it'll either clear the light or your mechanic may need to plug it in and reset parameters or do a forced regen to clear the fault.  You can repeat the process with another can if it really needs it, it won't do any harm at all to the filter, just loosen and dissolve the soot. Leave the pressure sensor tubes disconnected while you're cleaning the DPF, you don't want to risk any of the cleaner getting into the sensor itself (it's a strong caustic agent so wear gloves and eye protection when you're using it). Good luck!

Known too many people (ladies and blokes) who insisted it wasn't until it was almost too late to deal with easily, to ignore the fact that it could be - so please, please however inconvenient it may be right now - get that probability investigated asap.  (I haven't used the word 'possibility' deliberately)

If putting your chin down causes pain I would suspect a nerve issue rather than hamstring. When I had sciatica one of the suggested things to do was nerve flossing, where you sit in a chair and alternately raise your leg and your chin to get the nerve moving and hopefully "unstick" the irritated part.

My recent purchase of some cheap wide toed perfectly flat clogs have done wonders for my leg joints, hips and lower back. There wasn't all that much wrong to start with, but a few sharp twinges, little wobbles, having to hold on when stepping down or up - it was making me old and cautious. Two days after starting to wear the clogs I was standing straighter and moving around much more easily. Knees are not clunking, ankles not swelling, shoulders more flexible - nothing like a bit of stress and anxiety to tighten the shoulders and neck. There did not seem to be anything wrong with my old footwear - except it was old, but these soft foam clogs are an eye opener. If your problem could be associated with twisting of ligaments, stressing of joints and muscles it might be worth giving this sort of clog a try.
